evidence.snippet: (IPEX) Syndrome is a rare recessive disorder caused by mutations in the FOXP3
evidence.explanation: The IPEX cohort establishes FOXP3-associated immune dysregulation as a monogenic context in which enteropathy occurs.

evidence.snippet: FOXP3 is the key factor in human Treg development and competitiveness
evidence.explanation: Supports the atomic mechanism that FOXP3 disruption impairs the regulatory T-cell compartment.

steps/3.description: FOXP3-associated IPEX causes impaired regulatory T-cell development and function, weakening peripheral tolerance and permitting pathogenic effector-T-cell activity at mucosal surfaces.

evidence.snippet: More recently, mutations in LRBA have been reported as a cause of IPEX-like clinical manifestations characterized by early-onset enteropathy and endocrinopathies (35).

evidence.explanation: Supports an LRBA-associated Treg abnormality distinct from FOXP3 primary transcriptional deficiency.

steps/4.description: LRBA deficiency is modeled separately from FOXP3 and primary CTLA4 haploinsufficiency because it affects CTLA4 biology indirectly through intracellular trafficking and reduced Treg function in IPEX-like disease.

evidence.snippet: heterozygous mutation in CTLA4 resulting in CTLA4 haploinsufficiency, causing decreased capacity to mediate cell contact-dependent suppression
evidence.explanation: Supports CTLA4 haploinsufficiency as a distinct checkpoint mechanism impairing regulatory T-cell suppression.

evidence.snippet: In patients with CTLA4 deficiency the frequency of CD4+ Treg cells was normal or slightly decreased, suggesting that autoimmunity in these patients is caused by defective Treg function.
evidence.explanation: Supports that CTLA4-associated disease reflects defective Treg function, not simply absent Treg cells.

steps/5.description: CTLA4 haploinsufficiency causes defective regulatory T-cell checkpoint function, reducing cell-contact-dependent suppression and producing an IPEX-like immune-dysregulation phenotype with enteropathy.

evidence.explanation: Establishes GDAP1 as the CMT4A gene with both axonal and demyelinating phenotypes.

steps/6.description: Biallelic GDAP1 mutations (CMT4A) disrupt regulation of the mitochondrial network. GDAP1 promotes mitochondrial fission, and its loss impairs mitochondrial dynamics in Schwann cells and neurons, producing a neuropathy that can be axonal, demyelinating, or mixed and is frequently accompanied by vocal cord paresis.

evidence.snippet: A gene mutated in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4B (CMT4B), an autosomal recessive demyelinating neuropathy with myelin outfoldings, has been mapped on chromosome 11q22.
evidence.explanation: Establishes CMT4B as an autosomal recessive demyelinating neuropathy with myelin outfoldings; MTMR2 (CMT4B1) is the causal phosphoinositide phosphatase.

evidence.snippet: we identified two different nonsense mutations in the myotubularin-related 13 gene, MTMR13.
evidence.explanation: Establishes SBF2 / MTMR13 loss as the CMT4B2 lesion in the same myotubularin outfolding mechanism.

steps/7.description: Biallelic loss of the myotubularin-family phosphoinositide phosphatases MTMR2 (CMT4B1) and SBF2 / MTMR13 (CMT4B2) dysregulates Schwann-cell membrane phosphoinositide turnover. The resulting membrane-trafficking defect produces the redundant, focally folded (outfolded) myelin that is the histological hallmark of CMT4B, and a demyelinating neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: We subsequently identified mutations in an uncharacterized transcript, KIAA1985, in 12 families with autosomal recessive neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes SH3TC2 (KIAA1985) as the CMT4C gene across 12 autosomal recessive neuropathy families.

steps/8.description: Biallelic SH3TC2 (KIAA1985) mutations (CMT4C) disrupt an endosomal-recycling function required for normal Schwann-cell myelination, producing a childhood-onset demyelinating neuropathy with a distinct Schwann-cell pathology and prominent early-onset scoliosis.

evidence.snippet: HMSNL shows features of Schwann-cell dysfunction and a concomitant early axonal involvement, suggesting that impaired axon-glia interactions play a major role in its pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes impaired axon-glia interaction from Schwann-cell NDRG1 loss as the CMT4D (HMSN-Lom) mechanism.

evidence.snippet: L- and S-periaxin are proteins of myelinating Schwann cells and homozygous periaxin-null mice display extensive demyelination of myelinated fibers in the peripheral nervous system
evidence.explanation: Periaxin-null mice show extensive PNS demyelination, supporting periaxin's role in Schwann-cell myelin maintenance in CMT4F.

steps/9.description: Biallelic loss of Schwann-cell genes NDRG1 (CMT4D / HMSN-Lom) and PRX / periaxin (CMT4F) disrupts myelinating Schwann-cell function and the axon-glia interaction required to maintain the myelin sheath. NDRG1 loss produces Schwann-cell dysfunction with early axonal involvement, and periaxin loss destabilizes the myelin sheath, in both cases yielding a demyelinating neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: Autosomal recessive peripheral neuropathies are relatively rare but are clinically more severe than autosomal dominant forms of CMT
evidence.explanation: Supports the earlier-onset, more-severe clinical course that distinguishes the recessive CMT4 compartment from dominant CMT.

steps/10.description: The shared terminal node of the autosomal-recessive CMT4 compartment. The diverse Schwann-cell and neuronal lesions (GDAP1 mitochondrial dysfunction, myotubularin phosphoinositide dysregulation, SH3TC2 trafficking defect, NDRG1 and periaxin loss) converge on demyelination — often with redundant myelin outfoldings or onion-bulb formation — and, over time, length-dependent secondary axonal degeneration. It is this secondary axonal loss, affecting the longest motor and sensory fibers first, that produces the progressive distal clinical deficit shared across all CMT compartments, typically with earlier onset and greater severity in the recessive forms.

steps/1.description: In contrast to postsynaptic or synaptic CMS, resting (unstimulated) neuromuscular transmission in CMS6 is essentially normal: endplate AChR number, quantal content of the endplate potential, and miniature endplate potential (MEPP) amplitude are all normal at rest. The defect only manifests under sustained functional demand — after a conditioning train of high-frequency (10 Hz) nerve stimulation, MEPP amplitude falls (consistent with fewer ACh molecules per synaptic vesicle) because depleted synaptic vesicles cannot be adequately refilled with newly synthesized ACh. Neuromuscular junction ultrastructure is normal on electron microscopy.

The hypothesis is that the episignature is the visible trace of a genome-wide loss of ZNF699-directed repression, and that derepression of specific target genes during development produces the phenotype. The 2024 cohort's differentially-methylated-region analysis pointed at genes plausibly involved in pathogenesis but did not test any. Against the hypothesis: the episignature is measured in blood leukocytes, not in the developing organs; the KRAB-KAP1 axis has been validated structurally and functionally for other KRAB zinc finger proteins (ZNF93) but never for ZNF699; and no ZNF699 target has been identified. The hypothesis predicts that ZNF699-null cells would show derepression and hypomethylation at a definable set of loci and that those loci would be enriched for developmental regulators of the affected organs.

open_questions/0.rationale: This is the central unexplained fact of the disease, and it runs against the textbook. CD28 is the co-stimulatory receptor of the two-signal model, and losing it should produce a combined immunodeficiency; instead these patients have normal T cell development, normal leukocyte counts and immunoglobulins, carry EBV and CMV without disease, and are ill only from HPV-2 and HPV-4 in skin. The authors state the conclusion - CD28-dependent T cell responses are largely redundant for protective immunity - but not the reason. Candidate explanations that the published work does not distinguish between: the somatic revertant memory CD4+ T cell population may cover most requirements while being too small or wrongly localized to clear cutaneous papillomavirus; keratinocyte control of HPV may depend on a tissue-resident T cell response with an unusually strict co-stimulation requirement; or CD2 and other co-stimulatory routes, which these T cells use normally, may substitute everywhere except the skin. Nothing in the literature tests these against each other, and with three patients in one family there is little prospect of resolving it clinically.

So viral type, not host genotype, is doing the work here - but no comparison of HPV-2 and HPV-4 in a CD28-deficient background has been made, and the mouse model uses a third virus entirely. open_questions/2.rationale: The model is excellent for the immunological requirement and poor for the disease. It establishes that CD28, and specifically the CD28-CD80/CD86 axis, is required for papillomavirus control, since ligand blockade phenocopies the knockout. But the knockout's cutaneous warts regress spontaneously at about five weeks, mucosal clearance is delayed rather than absent, and the authors conclude that CD28 deficiency delays but does not prevent clearance. The human counterpart is a lesion that progressed to giant cutaneous horns over years. Papillomaviruses are strictly species-specific, so the discrepancy cannot be resolved by infecting mice with HPV-2; it needs either a humanized system or a mouse virus that establishes persistence in this background. Until then, the persistence and progression half of the human disease has no model, which is also the half any therapy would have to address.

steps/3.description: Dysregulated hyaluronan turnover during embryonic development disrupts morphogenesis of the tissues in which hyaluronan is a critical, transient matrix constituent - the craniofacial structures (palatal shelves, lip), the heart, the vitreous of the eye, and the skeleton - producing the orofacial clefting, cardiac malformations, myopia, and skeletal findings that define the syndrome. Mechanistically, failure to clear high-molecular-weight hyaluronan drives excess epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and decreased differentiation in the affected cushions and shelves. The Hyal2-/- mouse recapitulates these developmental abnormalities, supporting a causal, conserved role for HYAL2 in this process.

evidence.snippet: Here, we describe mutations in the HYAL2 gene as a cause of syndromic orofacial clefting.
evidence.explanation: Identifies syndromic orofacial clefting as the defining presentation of HYAL2 mutations.

evidence.explanation: Identifies extracellular hyaluronan degradation as the function of HYAL2, whose loss leaves that substrate incompletely turned over. This is a background statement of HYAL2 enzymology, not a human clinical observation, so it is graded OTHER.

evidence.explanation: Ties impaired hyaluronan turnover to the developing heart and palatal shelf matrix, the substrates of the affected morphogenesis. This is a background statement of HYAL2 enzymology, not a human clinical observation, so it is graded OTHER.

edges/4.description: Disrupted palatal shelf morphogenesis produces cleft palate.

evidence.snippet: There is no cure for HYAL2 deficiency. Supportive care to improve quality of life, maximize function, and reduce complications is recommended.

treatments/0.description: There is no cure for HYAL2 deficiency. Management is supportive, coordinated by a multidisciplinary team (pediatric cardiology and cardiac surgery for cardiac anomalies, a craniofacial team for the clefting, and audiology and speech-language pathology for hearing and communication) to maximize function and reduce complications.

evidence.snippet: care by specialists in pediatric cardiology and cardiac surgery and a multidisciplinary craniofacial team to coordinate timing and type of surgical interventions
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes cardiac surgery and coordinated craniofacial surgical interventions as part of management.

treatments/1.description: Surgical management is directed at the structural anomalies - staged craniofacial/cleft repair and cardiac surgery for the congenital cardiac anomalies (including cor triatriatum sinister when hemodynamically significant).

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Staged craniofacial/cleft surgery repairs the orofacial cleft, restoring the lip anatomy; symptomatic correction of the structural malformation rather than modification of the underlying developmental mechanism.

treatments/1/targets/1.description: Cleft palate repair restores palatal continuity for feeding and speech.

treatments/1/targets/2.description: Cardiac surgery corrects the congenital cardiac anomalies (including lesions requiring intervention in the first year of life).

treatments/1/targets/3.description: Surgical resection of the dividing left-atrial membrane corrects cor triatriatum sinister when hemodynamically significant.

evidence.snippet: Once the HYAL2 pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for relatives at risk and prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents the genetic counseling and testing options that follow from recessive inheritance.

evidence.snippet: each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being an asymptomatic carrier, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states the 25% sib recurrence risk that the genetic-counseling description reports.

treatments/2.description: Because HYAL2 deficiency is autosomal recessive, genetic counseling informs families of the 25% recurrence risk for sibs and the availability of carrier, prenatal, and preimplantation genetic testing once the familial variants are known.

evidence.snippet: a 50% to 66% decrease in hydroxymethylbilane synthase enzyme activity compared to normal
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the enzyme deficiency in the index adult kindred.

evidence.snippet: Erythrocyte HMBS activity was measured at 18% in our patient (and in her brother with the shared genotype and phenotype) and 50% in an asymptomatic sibling carrying a monoallelic variant.
evidence.explanation: Contrasts the profound biallelic enzyme deficit against the half-normal activity of an unaffected heterozygous sibling.

steps/1.description: Biallelic HMBS variants reduce hydroxymethylbilane synthase (porphobilinogen deaminase) activity, and the reported range is wide. The index kindred had a 50% to 66% decrease, so 34-50% residual activity — overlapping what heterozygous AIP carriers have. A separate adult kindred had 18% residual erythrocyte activity against 50% in an unaffected heterozygous sibling, and the infantile-onset cases are markedly reduced. So residual activity is not uniformly below the heterozygous range, and the severity gradient tracks the specific allele pair rather than biallelic status alone. This is the third enzyme of heme biosynthesis, converting porphobilinogen to hydroxymethylbilane.

evidence.snippet: Patients had a slight and moderate increase in urinary and plasma porphobilinogen and 5'-aminolevulinic acid, respectively
evidence.explanation: Documents the modest peripheral precursor elevation characteristic of the adult leukoencephalopathy phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Plasma and urine exhibited high concentrations of 5-aminolevulinic acid, porphobilinogen, and uroporphyrin 1.
evidence.explanation: Documents marked precursor accumulation in the severe infantile-onset presentation.

steps/2.description: 5-aminolevulinic acid, porphobilinogen, and uroporphyrin accumulate in plasma and urine. Accumulating porphobilinogen secondarily inhibits ALAD, which drives ALA higher still. In the adult leukoencephalopathy phenotype the peripheral elevation is only slight to moderate, well short of what an AIP attack produces — so the disease is not simply "more AIP".

evidence.snippet: We were not able to detect PBG in the CSF of patients unaffected by AIP.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that CSF porphobilinogen is a disease-associated finding rather than a normal constituent.

evidence.snippet: In his urine, 5-aminolevulinic acid and porphobilinogen were markedly elevated, but in cerebrospinal fluid just porphobilinogen.
evidence.explanation: Reports the CSF precursor profile in an independent severely affected case.

steps/3.description: Porphobilinogen and ALA are detectable and constitutively elevated in cerebrospinal fluid, and PBG is not detectable in the CSF of individuals without the disease. Critically, CSF levels are unchanged by liver transplantation, which means the central compartment is not simply receiving hepatically produced precursor. Whether the neurotoxic agent is the accumulated precursor or, alternatively, an absolute heme deficit in the CNS remains unsettled — see the knowledge gaps below.

evidence.snippet: Their brain MRIs show mainly confluent signal abnormalities in the periventricular and deep white matter and bilateral thalami.
evidence.explanation: Defines the anatomical distribution of the white matter lesion across six affected adults.

evidence.snippet: Findings at autopsy of the brain showed patchy gliosis and leukodystrophy.
evidence.explanation: Provides neuropathological confirmation of the leukodystrophy in the severe phenotype.

steps/4.description: A recognizable and consistent MRI pattern: confluent symmetrical signal abnormality of the periventricular and deep cerebral white matter and the bilateral thalami, with the central pons involved, progressing to cerebellar atrophy in advanced disease. In the severe infantile form the white matter change becomes cystic with progressive volume loss, and autopsy shows patchy gliosis and leukodystrophy.

evidence.snippet: All six affected individuals presented with slowly progressive spasticity, ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, with or without mild cognitive impairment, and/or ocular disease with onset in childhood or adolescence.
evidence.explanation: Reports progressive spasticity in all six adults in the largest published series.

steps/5.description: Slowly progressive spastic weakness of the lower limbs, present in every reported adult case and typically the presenting complaint.

evidence.snippet: Clinical features were childhood-onset slowly progressive spastic paraparesis, cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy
evidence.explanation: Reports cerebellar ataxia as a core feature of the index kindred.

steps/6.description: Progressive gait and limb ataxia, often with dysarthria, and quantifiable on ataxia rating scales over years.

evidence.snippet: All six affected individuals presented with slowly progressive spasticity, ataxia, peripheral neuropathy
evidence.explanation: Reports peripheral neuropathy in all six adults in the series.

steps/7.description: Length-dependent sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy of axonal type.

evidence.snippet: We identified 3 family members with a similar MRI pattern characterized by symmetrical signal abnormalities in the periventricular and deep cerebral white matter, thalami, and central part of the pons.
evidence.explanation: Describes the diagnostic MRI pattern in the index family.

steps/8.description: Symmetrical periventricular and deep cerebral white matter signal abnormality with thalamic and central pontine involvement; the recognizable imaging signature of the disorder.

evidence.snippet: Cerebellar atrophy was noted in advanced disease stages.
evidence.explanation: Records cerebellar atrophy as a late rather than presenting feature.

steps/9.description: Appears in advanced disease stages rather than at presentation.

evidence.explanation: Reports seizures in the infantile-onset severe presentation.

steps/11.description: A feature of the severe infantile-onset end of the spectrum, not of the adult leukoencephalopathy presentation.

evidence.snippet: Developmental delays and seizures persisted.
evidence.explanation: Records persistent developmental delay after attempted disease-modifying therapy.

steps/12.description: Severe, persistent developmental delay in the infantile-onset form, unimproved by liver transplantation.

evidence.snippet: Impaired conversion of PBG to hydroxymethylbilane leads to the accumulation of the precursors, PBG and ALA.
evidence.explanation: States the direct enzymatic consequence linking HMBS deficiency to precursor accumulation.

edges/1.description: Blocking the PBG-to-hydroxymethylbilane step backs up the pathway, accumulating porphobilinogen and, through secondary inhibition of ALAD, 5-aminolevulinic acid.

evidence.snippet: porphyrin precursor levels are constitutively elevated in the cerebrospinal fluid and are not reduced by haem arginate therapy
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the CNS precursor burden is constitutive rather than attack-driven or hepatically controlled.

edges/2.description: Precursors are present in the central compartment, and unlike in AIP their concentration there does not track hepatic heme synthesis.

edges/3.description: Sustained central exposure is the proposed driver of the white matter lesion, but the neuropathological mechanism connecting the two has not been established.

edges/4.description: Length-dependent sensorimotor axonal neuropathy accompanies the central lesion, paralleling the peripheral neuropathy of AIP.

evidence.snippet: Cerebellar atrophy was noted in advanced disease stages.
evidence.explanation: Establishes cerebellar atrophy as a late feature of the progressing lesion.

edges/8.description: Appears at advanced disease stages rather than at presentation, which is why it is drawn as a late consequence of the progressing lesion rather than a parallel finding.

edges/9.description: The mild cognitive impairment seen in some adults is attributed to the deep white matter disease, though the anatomical correlation has not been demonstrated.

edges/10.description: In the severe infantile form, where the white matter change becomes cystic. Not a feature of the adult presentation.

edges/11.description: In the severe infantile form. Persists after liver transplantation, which is consistent with fixed rather than ongoing injury.

evidence.snippet: Whole-exome sequencing revealed compound heterozygous missense variants in the HMBS gene, both associated with the autosomal dominant disorder acute intermittent porphyria.
evidence.explanation: Identifies HMBS as the causal gene and notes that the alleles are known AIP alleles.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) variants in HMBS, encoding hydroxymethylbilane synthase (porphobilinogen deaminase). The same gene in the monoallelic state causes autosomal dominant acute intermittent porphyria; several of the alleles found in biallelic leukoencephalopathy are themselves known AIP alleles, so the two disorders are allelic and distinguished by dose rather than by variant class.

evidence.snippet: Orthotopic liver transplantation at the age of 15 months led to only mild transient improvement.
evidence.explanation: Reports failure of liver transplantation to alter the disease course in the severe infantile form.

evidence.snippet: with only about a 50% reduction in the marked overproduction of ALA, PBG, and uroporphyrin, compared with his pre-transplant status
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the hepatic correction that transplantation did achieve in this patient. It refutes the therapy because halving precursor overproduction still did not arrest the neurological decline, which argues the residual source is not hepatic.

evidence.snippet: One individual reported here had improved neurological function for 12 months following liver transplantation followed by decline and progression of disease.
evidence.explanation: Records the transient benefit that motivated further attempts, before decline resumed; supports the intervention only as a temporary effect.

treatments/0.description: Attempted in several patients on the AIP rationale that replacing hepatic HMBS removes the precursor source. It does not work here, but the reason is sharper than "nothing changed". In one adult, precursor concentrations were unchanged in both compartments after transplantation. In an infant, hepatic correction was substantial - about a 50% reduction in ALA, PBG and uroporphyrin overproduction two years on - and the neurological decline continued anyway. Halving the hepatic output without arresting the disease is stronger evidence for an extrahepatic or CNS-autonomous precursor source than an absent biochemical response would be.

evidence.snippet: Liver transplantation and hepatically directed therapies are not likely to be effective for leukodystrophy due to biallelic HMBS variants.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly refutes the hepatic-source rationale for treating this disorder.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Intended to remove the hepatic source of porphyrin precursors; in this disorder it demonstrably fails to lower them.

evidence.snippet: A 5-day course of intravenous heme led to no observable clinical improvement.
evidence.explanation: Reports absence of clinical benefit from intravenous heme.

evidence.snippet: intravenous hematin, given daily for 5 days, had led to transient ∼50% reductions in urinary ALA, PBG, and porphyrins.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that haem does work biochemically in the peripheral compartment. Recorded as SUPPORT for the peripheral effect, which is what makes the absent central and clinical response a dissociation rather than simple inactivity.

treatments/1.description: Haem arginate or intravenous heme, the standard treatment for acute attacks in AIP, does work biochemically in the periphery - roughly 50% transient reductions in urinary ALA, PBG and porphyrins - but does not lower CSF porphyrin precursors and produces at most transient subjective clinical improvement. That dissociation is the point: the peripheral compartment responds and the central one does not, because parenterally administered heme does not reach the central nervous system. It is the same compartmental argument the liver transplantation entry makes.

evidence.snippet: porphyrin precursor levels are constitutively elevated in the cerebrospinal fluid and are not reduced by haem arginate therapy
evidence.explanation: Directly refutes that haem arginate lowers the central precursor burden.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Intended to suppress ALAS1 by negative feedback and so reduce precursor production; it does not reduce the central precursor burden.

evidence.snippet: Levetiracetam, which does not appear to exacerbate AIP, has been a welcome recent addition to the pharmacopoeia.
evidence.explanation: Identifies levetiracetam as the non-porphyrinogenic option, which is why it was the drug used.

evidence.snippet: He was treated with levetiracetam and phenobarbital.
evidence.explanation: Records the antiseizure regimen the infant was started on. Note this included phenobarbital, which was subsequently withdrawn - see the next item.

evidence.snippet: Because of the known risks of barbiturates in AIP, his medication regimen was adjusted, including tapering off phenobarbital, which is well-known to increase hepatic ALA synthase-1 and over-production of ALA and PBG
evidence.explanation: The drug-safety reversal. Phenobarbital was tapered off precisely because barbiturates induce hepatic ALAS1; without this the entry would appear to endorse a barbiturate under a treatment named for non-porphyrinogenic agents.

treatments/2.description: Seizures in the infantile-onset form require antiseizure drugs, and the choice is constrained by porphyria pharmacology: many older anticonvulsants induce hepatic heme synthesis and are avoided in porphyria. Levetiracetam does not appear to exacerbate AIP and was used in the reported infant, who was also started on phenobarbital and then tapered off it precisely because barbiturates induce hepatic ALAS1. Note that the rationale is inherited from AIP practice rather than demonstrated in this disorder, where hepatic induction is not the driver - which makes the case for avoiding barbiturates here weaker in principle than in AIP, though it was acted on.

evidence.snippet: No effective disease-modifying therapy currently exists for biallelic HMBS deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that no disease-modifying option is available, leaving supportive care as the standard.

treatments/3.description: In the absence of disease-modifying therapy, management is symptomatic: antiepileptic drugs, spasticity and ataxia management, rehabilitation, and visual support.

evidence.snippet: the heme precursors 5-aminolevulinic acid or porphobilinogen originating from the liver or central nervous system could be causative, and absolute heme deficiency in the central nervous system is another hypothesis
evidence.explanation: States both competing hypotheses as unresolved in the current literature.

evidence.snippet: Patients with Doss porphyria, caused by biallelic pathogenic ALAD variants, show high elevations of ALA and coproporphyrin but not of PBG and uroporphyrin. They often exhibit severe peripheral polyneuropathy, but they do not develop an affection of the CNS.
evidence.explanation: The human biallelic natural experiment this rationale argues from. ALA elevation without PBG elevation gives peripheral neuropathy and no CNS disease, which is what makes PBG the likelier of the two precursors.

evidence.snippet: The similarity in the potency and mechanism of the ALA-induced inhibition of muscimol binding in rat and human membranes indicate that rat studies are useful to evaluate the neurotoxic properties of ALA towards the human GABAergic system
evidence.explanation: Gives the precursor-toxicity arm of this gap a concrete molecular candidate - ALA antagonism of the GABA-A receptor, shown in human as well as rat cortical membranes. Indirect for this disorder because the experiment used millimolar ALA on synaptic membranes from unaffected brain, and was framed around acute intermittent porphyria rather than the constitutive, white-matter-predominant biallelic disease; whether the concentrations reached in LENCEP cerebrospinal fluid approach this range has not been measured.

open_questions/0.rationale:
These are the two standing hypotheses and they are not equivalent therapeutically: precursor toxicity would motivate an agent that lowers ALA/PBG inside the CNS, whereas a central heme deficit would require heme or a heme surrogate that crosses into the brain, which parenteral heme does not. The failure of both liver transplantation and haem arginate to alter CSF precursor levels or the clinical course is consistent with either, so the therapeutic failures do not discriminate between them. The edge from central precursor exposure to white matter degeneration is recorded as INDIRECT for this reason.
Two natural experiments narrow it without closing it. Doss porphyria, caused by biallelic ALAD variants, raises ALA but not PBG and produces severe peripheral polyneuropathy with no CNS involvement - so ALA elevation alone appears insufficient for white matter disease, and PBG becomes the likelier candidate of the two precursors. Separately, the PBGD-deficient mouse develops a chronic progressive neuropathy while ALA is normal or only twofold raised, which its authors read as implicating heme deficiency. The two point in different directions, which is why the gap stays open.

open_questions/1.rationale: Two mouse models exist and are curated in animal_models, but neither reproduces the white matter lesion. The PBGD-deficient mouse models the peripheral axonal neuropathy; the biallelic R167Q mouse reproduces the constitutive central precursor elevation and the haem non-response but has normal CNS histopathology, so it explicitly does not reproduce the white matter lesion. So what is missing specifically is a model of the leukodystrophy - a system in which CNS precursor concentrations can be raised or lowered independently of hepatic heme synthesis while the white matter is watched. That is also the platform any CNS-penetrant precursor-lowering strategy would need.

evidence.snippet: However, parenterally administered heme, which is effective in acute intermittent porphyria, does not reach the central nervous system.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the pharmacological barrier that makes AIP therapies inapplicable here.

open_questions/2.rationale: Givosiran, the ALAS1 siRNA that prevents attacks in AIP, is hepatically targeted, and access was declined for one post-transplant patient on exactly that ground. Since CSF precursors do not fall after liver transplantation, there is no reason to expect a liver-directed siRNA to reach the relevant compartment either. A CNS-penetrant strategy is what this disorder needs and none has been reported.

open_questions/3.rationale: Residual enzyme activity conferred by the specific allele pair is the presumed determinant, but with fewer than fifteen reported individuals the genotype-phenotype relationship rests on very few observations, and intrafamilial variability has been noted even for identical genotypes.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrate here that mutations in ATP6B1, encoding the B-subunit of the apical proton pump mediating distal nephron acid secretion, cause distal renal tubular acidosis
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease assignment from the study that made it. ATP6B1 is the former symbol for ATP6V1B1.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to the ubiquitous expression of most other vH+-ATPase subunits, expression of the B1 and a4 subunits appears to be primarily restricted to the inner ear and kidney
evidence.explanation: The restricted expression that explains why this subunit produces a two-organ disease rather than a systemic pump failure.

steps/1.description: Loss of the B1 subunit of the V1 cytosolic domain of the vacuolar H+-ATPase. B1 is one of the few V-ATPase subunits whose expression is essentially restricted to kidney and inner ear, which is precisely why a defect in it produces a two-organ disease rather than a systemic one - the ubiquitous pumps elsewhere use a different B isoform and are unaffected.

evidence.snippet: The vacuolar (v)H+-ATPase pump is one of the key membrane transporters for acid excretion in the α-intercalated cells of the distal nephron, and it is also expressed in the inner ear where it functions in endolymph pH homeostasis
evidence.explanation: States both roles of the same pump in one sentence, which is the basis for branching here rather than chaining.

steps/2.description: The pump cannot move protons across the apical membrane. This single failure is the branch point of the entry: the same defective transport step is read out as acidosis in the kidney and as deafness in the ear, and neither is downstream of the other.

evidence.snippet: a condition characterized by impaired renal acid secretion resulting in metabolic acidosis
evidence.explanation: Defines the renal lesion as impaired acid secretion producing metabolic acidosis.

steps/3.description: The collecting duct cannot acidify the tubular lumen, so acid generated by metabolism is retained. The signature is an inappropriately alkaline urine in the face of systemic acidosis - the urine pH will not fall below roughly 5.3 no matter how acidotic the blood becomes, which is what distinguishes a distal tubular defect from other causes of acidosis.

evidence.snippet: consistent with this finding, we demonstrate expression of ATP6B1 in cochlea and endolymphatic sac
evidence.explanation: The expression evidence that located the second branch anatomically.

evidence.snippet: Our data, together with the known requirement for active proton secretion to maintain proper endolymph pH, implicate ATP6B1 in endolymph pH homeostasis and in normal auditory function.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own statement of the inference, which is an argument from expression plus known physiology rather than a direct measurement of endolymph pH in patients.

steps/4.description: The endolymph of the inner ear is an unusual extracellular fluid whose ionic and pH composition must be actively maintained, and the same B1-containing pump does that maintenance. This is the second, independent branch of the disease - it is not a consequence of acidosis, and patients can have it with the renal phenotype barely apparent.

evidence.snippet: an autosomal recessive disorder of renal H+transport causing a buildup of acid in the bloodstream (metabolic acidosis) with associated alkaline urine
evidence.explanation: Pairs the systemic acidosis with the inappropriately alkaline urine that identifies its distal tubular origin.

steps/5.description: Normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with hypokalaemia. The chronic acid load is then buffered at the expense of bone mineral and shifts urinary chemistry toward stone formation, which is how a transport defect in one cell type ends up causing rickets and nephrocalcinosis.

evidence.snippet: Distal renal tubular acidosis (DRTA) is characterized by tubular defects in urinary acidification and hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia, nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis.
evidence.explanation: Lists the full downstream cluster this node represents - hypercalciuria and hypocitraturia as the urinary chemistry, nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis as the structural result.

steps/6.description: Calcium deposition in the renal parenchyma with stone formation, and rickets or osteomalacia with growth failure. These are the manifestations that untreated disease accumulates over time, and the ones alkali therapy is given to prevent.

evidence.snippet: MRL-Atp6v1b1vtx/vtx mutant mice exhibit profound hearing impairment, which is associated with enlarged endolymphatic compartments of the inner ear
evidence.explanation: Ties the hearing loss to enlarged endolymphatic compartments in a model carrying a spontaneous Atp6v1b1 mutation. Typed MODEL_ORGANISM because the measurement is in mice.

steps/7.description: Enlarged endolymphatic compartments - seen radiologically as an enlarged vestibular aqueduct - with sensorineural hearing loss that progresses over time. Onset and severity vary considerably between patients carrying comparable variants, and the mouse work below suggests genetic background is part of why.

edges/1.description: The subunit is part of the pump that performs the secretion, so losing it removes the activity.

edges/2.description: In the collecting duct the lost activity is the acid-secreting step itself.

edges/3.description: In the inner ear the same pump maintains endolymph pH, so its loss acts there independently of anything happening in the kidney.

edges/4.description: Retained acid titrates plasma bicarbonate, and the compensatory distal sodium handling drives potassium loss.

edges/5.description: Bone and stone consequences follow from sustained systemic acidosis rather than from the pump defect acting locally.

edges/6.description: The route from disturbed endolymph pH to enlarged endolymphatic compartments and cochlear dysfunction is not established in detail; the association is firm, the intermediate steps are not.

evidence.snippet: Our study shows that rare and family-specific variants in ATP6V1B1 are responsible for DRTA and sensorineural hearing loss syndrome in Turkey.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the private, family-specific allelic architecture of the recessive form.

evidence.snippet: All mutations were homozygous in affected children and co-segregated as a fully penetrant autosomal recessive trait in each family.
evidence.explanation: Segregation supporting causation and full penetrance in the recessive form.

genes/0.notes:
Encodes the B1 subunit of the V1 cytosolic domain of the vacuolar H+-ATPase. Variants reported in the recessive families are private and family-specific rather than recurrent - nonsense, missense and frameshift alleles across the coding sequence - so there is no founder allele to test for and full gene sequencing is required.
The one recurrent position is Arg394, and it behaves differently: heterozygous variants there act dominantly, which is curated as a subtype above.

evidence.snippet: While early treatment corrects the biochemical abnormalities and helps to foster normal growth, deafness appears not to be prevented.
evidence.explanation: The single most important treatment statement for this entry: alkali corrects the renal arm and does not touch the auditory one. That is the clinical consequence of the two-arm architecture, and it is now evidenced rather than asserted in prose.

evidence.snippet: The aims of the treatment of DRTA must be to correct biochemical abnormalities, improve growth and prevent nephrocalcinosis that can lead to chronic renal failure and skeletal abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: States the therapeutic goals, which are the renal and growth consequences rather than the hearing loss.

evidence.snippet: While hypercalciuria with nephrocalcinosis is seen in almost all cases, renal function usually remains normal with proper and early treatment.
evidence.explanation: PARTIAL because it qualifies the outcome rather than the treatment: nephrocalcinosis still occurs in nearly everyone, and what early treatment preserves is renal function rather than preventing the calcification.

treatments/0.description:
Oral alkali - bicarbonate or citrate salts - given to correct the systemic acidosis the kidney cannot correct itself. Citrate preparations do double duty, since urinary citrate is also the inhibitor of calcium precipitation that is depleted in this disease, so replacing it addresses both the acidosis and the stone risk.
It corrects the consequence, not the cause: the pump remains defective and the urine remains inappropriately alkaline. It also does nothing for the ear, because the auditory branch is not downstream of the acidosis.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replaces the buffer the kidney fails to regenerate, addressing the systemic consequence rather than the transport defect.

treatments/1.description: Amplification or cochlear implantation as the hearing loss progresses. Curated as a separate treatment from alkali therapy because it addresses a separate branch of the disease - correcting the acidosis has no effect on the ear. The serial audiometry that decides when to escalate is curated under diagnosis#Audiologic Assessment, so this record covers the intervention rather than the monitoring.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Compensates for the auditory deficit; it does not act on endolymph homeostasis.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Potassium-sparing diuretics should be used with caution or avoided.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews Management names the drug class to avoid in hereditary dRTA.

treatments/2.description: GeneReviews lists potassium-sparing diuretics among the agents to use with caution or avoid. This is counterintuitive at first sight, because the disease runs with hypokalemia and a potassium-sparing agent looks corrective - but the defect is in distal proton secretion, which these drugs impair further, so the acidosis worsens while the potassium is being chased.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Avoidance is aimed at not compounding the primary transport lesion; it does not correct it.

evidence.snippet: ADV7103 is a combination controlled-release potassium bicarbonate and potassium citrate medication approved in Europe that allows less frequent dosing.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews Management statement naming the product, its composition, its approval status and its practical advantage.

treatments/3.description:
A combination controlled-release potassium bicarbonate and potassium citrate preparation, approved in Europe. Its value is adherence rather than a new mechanism: conventional alkali must be taken several times daily including overnight to hold the correction, and this formulation allows less frequent dosing.

It is curated separately from generic alkali because it is a named, regulator-approved product for this indication rather than a class, and because the dosing interval is the practical obstacle to treating a lifelong condition that begins in infancy.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Same buffer replacement as conventional alkali, delivered on a schedule patients can sustain.

open_questions/0.rationale:
This is not an absence of evidence - there are two well-characterised models and they were carefully phenotyped. The problem is that neither reproduces the two-organ disease that defines the human condition, and the reasons differ. The C57BL/6 knockout escapes the renal phenotype through documented compensatory relocalisation of B2-containing pumps to the apical membrane, and has normal hearing. The MRL spontaneous mutant is profoundly deaf with enlarged endolymphatic compartments but still has no overt acidosis, and its deafness disappears on a B6 background.
Two consequences follow. Any preclinical test of a therapy for the renal branch is being run in an animal that has already compensated for the defect being treated. And the strain-dependence of the auditory phenotype is a live hypothesis for the unexplained variability in hearing loss among human patients with comparable variants - the mapped Chr 13 locus explains only about 20% of the variance, so the modifier architecture is largely unknown in mice and entirely unknown in humans.

open_questions/1.rationale:
If a dominant-negative subunit poisons the pump complex, one might expect it to affect both tissues that depend on that complex. Instead hearing loss was reported in only about a third of the dominant Arg394 patients, against severe congenital or early-onset loss in essentially all affected individuals in the recessive cohorts.
Several explanations are available and none is established: residual wild-type subunit may be sufficient for the ear but not the kidney, the two tissues may differ in how much B2 substitution they tolerate, or the ear may be more sensitive to total absence than to a poisoned complex. Distinguishing these would say something general about how much pump activity each organ actually requires - a quantitative question the two-organ structure of this disease is unusually well placed to answer.

evidence.snippet: Segmental arterial mediolysis is a vascular disease of putative vasospastic origin that causes massive hemorrhages.
evidence.explanation: This supports the vasospastic origin model while preserving its putative rather than proven causal status.

steps/0.description: SAM is hypothesized to begin with a vasospastic arterial insult that injures the arterial media rather than a primary inflammatory arteritis or atherosclerotic process.

evidence.snippet: Pathologic correlations reveal that lytic loss of medial muscle causes arterial dilatation, dilated arterial gaps form aneurysms, dissections develop at arterial-medial gap junctions or from reparative granulation tissue and reparative alterations, and thrombi cause stenosis and occlusions.
evidence.explanation: This directly connects medial muscle loss to the major imaging and clinical vascular sequelae.

steps/1.description: Lytic loss of arterial medial smooth muscle weakens the vessel wall and creates arterial gaps that evolve into dilatation, aneurysm, dissection, stenosis, or occlusion.

evidence.snippet: The most common radiologic findings at onset are aneurysms, arterial dilatation, and occlusions, while dissections and stenotic lesions often are delayed.
evidence.explanation: This supports temporal evolution from early dilatation/occlusion to delayed dissecting and stenotic lesions.

steps/2.description: After the injurious phase, reparative granulation tissue, fibrosis, and thrombus can remodel the arterial wall, sometimes stabilizing lesions and sometimes producing stenosis or occlusion.

evidence.snippet: The most commonly affected vessels were the superior mesenteric (53%), hepatic (45%), celiac (36%), renal (26%), and splenic (25%) arteries with aneurysm (76%), dissection (61%), and arterial rupture (46%).
evidence.explanation: The systematic review supports the main affected vessels and the high frequency of aneurysm.

steps/3.description: SAM produces multifocal visceral arterial aneurysms, often involving renal, superior mesenteric, celiac, hepatic, and splenic arteries.

evidence.snippet: The most common imaging findings were dissection (86%), aneurysm (57%), beading or webs (28%), occlusion (19%), and a rind or wall thickening (15%).
evidence.explanation: This directly supports arterial dissection as the most common imaging finding in the large SAM imaging cohort.

steps/4.description: SAM commonly produces visceral arterial dissections, a distinct vascular lesion from aneurysm or dilatation.

evidence.snippet: Abdominal pain (80%) and intraabdominal bleeding (50%) were the most common presenting symptoms.
evidence.explanation: This supports intra-abdominal bleeding as a major clinical presentation.

steps/5.description: Rupture of affected arteries can cause intra-abdominal bleeding or severe hemorrhage.

evidence.snippet: Abdominal computerized tomography showed arterial thickening, arterial dilatations, and dissections of the splenic and renal arteries, leading to organ ischemia.
evidence.explanation: This case-review abstract directly links SAM arterial lesions to organ ischemia.

steps/6.description: Dissection, stenosis, or occlusion in visceral or renal arteries can cause ischemic injury to supplied organs.

edges/0.description: Vasospastic or hypoxic injury is thought to trigger focal loss of medial smooth muscle integrity.

evidence.snippet: The most common imaging findings were dissection (86%), aneurysm (57%), beading or webs (28%), occlusion (19%), and a rind or wall thickening (15%).
evidence.explanation: This imaging cohort identifies dissection and aneurysm as the dominant lesion types at presentation.

edges/1.description: Arterial gaps and medial weakening produce dilatation, aneurysm, and dissection.

evidence.snippet: The most common imaging findings were dissection (86%), aneurysm (57%), beading or webs (28%), occlusion (19%), and a rind or wall thickening (15%).
evidence.explanation: This imaging cohort identifies dissection as the most frequent imaging finding in SAM.

edges/2.description: Arterial-medial gap junctions can evolve into arterial dissection.

edges/3.description: Flow-limiting stenosis, occlusion, dissection, and rupture can cause ischemic organ injury or life-threatening bleeding.

edges/4.description: Arterial rupture can cause life-threatening intra-abdominal bleeding.

evidence.snippet: After diagnosis of SAM, aspirin was prescribed in 60.7% (n = 71). Statins were prescribed in 29.9% (n = 35). Antihypertensive medications were prescribed in 65% (n = 76), including beta blockers in 42.7% (n = 50); 40.2% (n = 47) of patients were prescribed anticoagulation.
evidence.explanation: This cohort supports common real-world medical management with antiplatelet, statin, antihypertensive, and anticoagulant therapy.

evidence.snippet: Follow-up imaging is required to monitor for disease progression.
evidence.explanation: This conclusion supports surveillance imaging after diagnosis.

treatments/0.description: Stable patients are often managed with blood-pressure control, individualized antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, analgesia, and serial vascular imaging to detect regression, stability, or progression.

evidence.snippet: Of the 17 patients undergoing endovascular intervention, 19 procedures were performed, most commonly embolization
evidence.explanation: This cohort identifies embolization as the dominant endovascular intervention.

treatments/1.description: Endovascular treatment is used for selected unstable, bleeding, enlarging, or anatomically treatable lesions, most often by embolization.

evidence.snippet: followed by stenting
evidence.explanation: This cohort supports stenting as a distinct but less common endovascular intervention.

treatments/2.description: Stenting is a less frequent endovascular option for selected SAM lesions.

evidence.snippet: Of the 13 patients undergoing open surgery, 14 procedures were performed, including arterial bypass
evidence.explanation: This cohort supports open surgery and organ surgery as selected interventions in SAM.

treatments/3.description: Open repair, bypass, thrombectomy, aneurysm ligation, or organ surgery is reserved for patients with uncontrolled hemorrhage, ischemia, anatomy not suitable for endovascular therapy, or complications requiring operative management.
